sections.content: You know the conditional for advice and polite requests (*podría*) from A2 Unit 26, and the conditional of probability for guesses about the past from B1 Unit 22. The press uses the conditional a third way: to pass on information it has not confirmed. *El alcalde habría dimitido* means "The mayor has reportedly resigned": the writer reports the claim but does not stand behind it. Use *habría* + a past participle for something that already happened, and the simple conditional for how things are said to stand now (*Los daños serían importantes*). Markers often go with it: *según fuentes*, *al parecer* (B2 Unit 18) and *presuntamente*. Some style guides advise against this use and prefer to name the source (*según la policía*), so treat it as a convention to recognise and use with care.

sections.title: One form, four jobs
rows: Could you help me? (a polite request)
It was probably ten when he arrived. (your own guess)
The mayor has reportedly resigned. (a claim you cannot confirm)
The damage is reportedly serious. (a claim about now)

items.spanish: Según fuentes, el alcalde habría dimitido.
items.english: According to sources, the mayor has reportedly resigned.

items.spanish: Al parecer, el incendio habría comenzado en el almacén.
items.english: Apparently the fire is reported to have started in the warehouse.

items.spanish: Los daños serían importantes, pero aún no hay confirmación.
items.english: The damage is reportedly serious, but there is no confirmation yet.
The mayor has resigned. (stated as a fact)

sections.content: English uses a word or a passive for this: *reportedly*, *is said to have*. Spanish puts it in the verb, so *habría dimitido* is not "would have resigned". When you can confirm a fact, use the indicative (*El alcalde ha dimitido*), and when you can, name the source (*según la policía*) instead of relying on the conditional.
